title: The Hanseatic League: Trade Without Kings

cards.b:
From the 1200s to the 1600s, merchant towns across northern Europe formed a loose network called the Hanseatic League. It had no king, no army of its own and no single capital. Yet it shaped trade from London to Novgorod.

The Hanseatic story shows how commerce, city law and shared rules could build a power that rivalled kings.

The city of Lübeck, on the Baltic coast of northern Germany, was the centre of the League. Its merchants developed trade rules and a shared legal code, the Lübeck law, which was copied by many towns. Hamburg, Bremen and Danzig became important partners.

The League met in assemblies called Hansetage. Member towns decided on common rules, trade privileges and, when needed, joint action against rivals.

The Hanseatic merchants ran trading posts, called kontors, in key cities. These included the Steelyard in London, the Peterhof in Novgorod, the Bryggen in Bergen and a post in Bruges. The posts were like small walled communities with their own rules.

The kontors gave the League control over the trade in fish, grain, timber, furs and wax. Bergen's dried cod and Baltic grain flowed through the same network.

cards.h: Philippe Dollinger and the German Hansa
cards.b:
Philippe Dollinger, The German Hansa (1964)

Dollinger's classic study shows how the League worked in practice. He describes the trade routes, the member towns and the disputes that shaped their policy.

The book is still a standard guide, although later historians have added many new views.

cards.h: The Hanseatic League in key dates
cards.b: The League was at its strongest in the 14th and 15th centuries. Its decline came as new states and new trade routes took its place.

In the 1360s the League fought a war against King Valdemar IV of Denmark, who had taken control of Scania and threatened Baltic trade. The League won, and the 1370 Peace of Stralsund gave its members new trading privileges.

The war showed that the League could act as a naval and political power. It could choose kings and make peace, even without a single state behind it.

cards.h: Was the Hanseatic League a state?
cards.b:
Many people picture the League as a kind of medieval state, with a government and an army. The idea makes it easier to compare with modern nations.

Historians argue that the League was an association of towns and merchants, with shared rules but no central authority. Its members were often rivals. It is better described as a network than as a country.

Bergen's dried cod was sent south to feed Catholic Europe on fast days. Baltic grain and timber fed growing cities in the west, and furs and wax came from the eastern forests. Each good had its own trade route and its own rules.

The trade was profitable and organised. The Hanseatic merchants were shrewd, and they controlled the sale and quality of their goods with strict rules.

The League faded from the 1500s to the 1600s. Some historians point to the rise of strong territorial states, such as Sweden, Denmark and Russia, that controlled trade themselves. Others point to the shift of trade to the Atlantic.

The decline was gradual. Historians argue about the causes, but the League never completely vanished, and the names of its cities still mark the Hanseatic past.

The Peterhof in Novgorod was a major Hanseatic base. Russian princes allowed the merchants to trade there, and the merchants shipped furs, wax and honey to the West. The link was an early sign of Russia's place in European trade.

The relationship was not always peaceful. Disputes over rights and justice were common, and both sides used the courts to protect their interests.

In 1329 the Delhi Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced a copper token currency. The coins were meant to replace silver, but they were easy to forge, and trade collapsed. The king had to withdraw the tokens.

The Hanseatic towns were built on silver and trust. Muhammad's token money failed because people did not trust the paper of the state. The contrast shows how much coinage depended on confidence.

Five things to remember
  1. The League was a network of merchant towns, not a state.
  2. Lübeck was its centre.
  3. Kontors in London, Bergen, Bruges and Novgorod were its trading bases.
  4. The 1370 Peace of Stralsund gave it new privileges.
  5. It faded from the 1500s to the 1600s.
Think about it
  • Can a network of towns be as powerful as a king?
  • What holds a trading alliance together when it has no army?
